On 16-17 July 2026 in Washington, DC, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, met with US senators, participated in a ministerial meeting hosted by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, met with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Israel, ministers from South American countries, as well as White House and US administration officials and the leaders of the Joint Baltic American National Committee (JBANC). Conference on Countering Terrorism Romania - Ministry of Foreign Affairs Type: Press release Date: 07/16/26 During her visit to the United States, Romania's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Oana Țoiu, participated in ceremonies marking the presence of the Romanian training ship Mircea in the United States as part of the events commemorating the 250th anniversary of the adoption of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. She also met with Romanian students studying at Harvard University. The visit included hosting a roundtable discussion at the Atlantic Council focused on the next steps following the NATO Summit in Ankara, as well as on Romania-U.S. cooperation in the fields of economic development and security. The Minister of Foreign Affairs held meetings with Members of the U.S. Congress, including Senator Steve Daines, Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee on Europe; Representatives Mike Rogers and Pat Harrington, Chairman and Member, respectively, of the House Armed Services Committee; Representative Joe Wilson, Co-Chair of the U.S. Helsinki Commission; Representative Gregory Meeks of New York; and Representative Kevin Self of Texas. Discussions focused on the outcomes of the NATO Summit, the presence of U.S. troops in Romania, increasing bilateral investment and economic partnerships, and strengthening cooperation between Romanian and American companies. This autumn, Romania will host for the first time the Romania-United States Exchange Program, welcoming a delegation of congressional staff and representatives of leading U.S. think tanks. The program follows the agreement concluded this spring between the Romanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the U.S. Department of State. On 16 July, Minister Oana Țoiu will participate in the Ministerial Conference on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism, at the invitation of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. During the conference, she will present historical examples from Romania's experience in which political violence was used as an instrument by totalitarian regimes. Romania's painful experience with political repression, imprisonment, and state-sponsored crimes reinforces its commitment today to an agenda focused on prevention—addressing the conditions that enable political violence to take root, regardless of the ideology that seeks to legitimize violence as a political tool. The Minister will also present the European Union's perspective, drawing on the ProtectEU: European Internal Security Strategy, highlighting the need to strengthen efforts to prevent the online radicalization of young people and to enhance cooperation in preventing and countering terrorism.

The package aims to impose tariffs on countries that continue buying Russian oil and gas or assist Moscow in circumventing existing sanctions. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna welcomed the Senate initiative, stressing that approval of the sanctions package would deal a significant blow to Russia's economy. "Energy exports play a central role in financing Russia's war machine, accounting for nearly one third of the aggressor's state budget," Tsahkna said. "Late Senator Lindsey Graham proposed imposing tariffs on countries that contribute to Russia's aggression or facilitate the operations of its shadow fleet. This is an important step that directly undermines Russia's economic capacity and reduces the revenue Moscow can channel into continuing its aggression against Ukraine. We commend the U.S. senators for this groundbreaking proposal." According to Tsahkna, the international community — including the European Union and the United States — must continue exerting pressure on Moscow until Russia stops bombing Ukraine and killing civilians, abandons its imperial ambitions, and takes accountability for the crimes it has committed. He emphasized that EU member states must overcome the current deadlock and approve a robust 21st sanctions package, which would, among other measures, keep the price cap on Russian crude oil at a consistently low level. "Sanctions and international isolation are working: Russia's economy is clearly deteriorating, internal tensions are rising, and Ukraine is achieving significant strategic gains on the battlefield. Russia will not abandon its aggressive course until countermeasures inflict truly painful consequences. Pressure on the aggressor must therefore remain steady and unwavering. This is not the moment for concessions," Tsahkna stressed. In addition to measures targeting countries that import Russian energy, the sanctions package includes restrictions on Russian President Vladimir Putin, other senior officials, financial institutions, state-owned enterprises, and companies supporting Russia's defense industry. The next step is approval by the full Senate.

http://www.heraldglobe.com/news/27919542.text: EU plugs budget hole with Google mega-fine RT.com 18 Jul 2026, 13:58 GMT+10 The 4.6 billion payment comes as the bloc continues to pour money into Ukraine and boost military spending The EU is set to use a multibillion-euro antitrust fine imposed on Google to help ease pressure on the bloc's budget after years of increased military spending and aid for Ukraine. The US tech giant has paid €4.6 billion ($5.4 billion), including interest, after losing a years-long legal battle over restrictions linked to its Android operating system. The sum is equivalent to more than 2% of the EU's 2026 budget. The European Commission imposed the fine in 2018, accusing Google of abusing Android's market dominance by requiring smartphone makers to pre-install Google Search and Chrome. Earlier this month, the EU's top court upheld the penalty, clearing the way for the payment. Under EU budget rules, fines collected by the commission are paid into the bloc's common budget, reducing the gross national income-based contributions required from member states. The windfall will not provide any direct relief for taxpayers, however, as European governments continue to scale back social spending while increasing military budgets and financing Ukraine. The EU deficit is projected to reach 3.6% of GDP by 2027. Despite the fiscal strain, Brussels has approved a €90 billion Ukraine support loan for 2026-2027, even as Kiev remains embroiled in repeated corruption scandals involving senior officials and figures close to Vladimir Zelensky. NATO members have also pledged €70 billion in military aid, training, and equipment for Ukraine this year, with plans to maintain similar support in 2027. At the same time, European governments have been urged to sharply increase military spending, with Brussels citing an alleged Russian threat to justify its rearmament drive. Moscow has dismissed the claims as "nonsense" designed to legitimize ballooning military budgets at the expense of social programs. The shift is already visible in national budgets. France, for example, has cut around €9 billion from several ministries while allocating an additional €6.5 billion to the military. Critics in several EU countries, including Hungary and Slovakia, argue that Brussels is shifting the cost of its unconditional backing for a corruption-plagued Ukraine onto ordinary Europeans. Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban has called the EU's Ukraine policy a "financial tragedy," while Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has labeled plans to phase out Russian energy "economic suicide" and vowed to oppose further military loans for Kiev. (Image: Bloomberg) Hungary’s $20 billion electric-vehicle industry, which has long enjoyed the protection of former premier Viktor Orban, is facing a reckoning as the country’s new leadership cracks down on environmental violations and looks to raise taxes. The government plans to introduce the strictest environmental rules in the European Union, hiking levies on polluters and ending lavish tax breaks for multinational companies, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said late Friday. The steps are part of a broad overhaul to rebalance corporate taxation, he said. That’s putting businesses from China in particular on notice, a country that’s bet big on Hungary as a springboard to the EU market and which has set up some of the biggest battery plants there, as well as EV leader BYD Co.’s first factory in the bloc. They’ve been among the biggest beneficiaries of Hungarian subsidies. Magyar’s landslide election win in April was powered partly by a grassroots backlash against battery factories and concerns about land, air and water pollution after years of lax enforcement under Orban’s 16-year rule. One of Orban’s first moves after his return to power in 2010 was to scrap the environment ministry. “There is no compromise, there is no flexibility in terms of adhering to all the environmental rules,” Transportation Minister David Vitezy told Bloomberg in an interview. “This government won’t look away at any point just because of Chinese industrial interest if they don’t adhere to all Hungarian laws.” Related Stories China floods back into India's fertiliser market, offering cheaper supplies than UAE, Algeria, Egypt China's Wild Siberian tigers rise to 72 and Amur Leopards reach 115 after 10 years of conservation�... China backs India to hold ‘successful’ BRICS summit but remains evasive about Xi’s attendance The signs of change are visible. Last month, the government suspended the operation of Semcorp, a Chinese producer of lithium-ion battery separator films for the EV industry, after finding that the groundwater under the factory had been contaminated. Semcorp is located in the industrial park that rings the eastern city of Debrecen, a longtime Orban stronghold that’s slipped from his influence due to mounting anger over battery plants. Semcorp didn’t reply to a request for comment. Next door to Semcorp, Chinese battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. is finishing its $8.4 billion plant, the biggest single investment in Hungary’s history. It too is facing a probe over suspected polluting after a greenish liquid bubbled up around the plant in May. CATL, in a statement to Bloomberg, said water had been colored with a non-toxic as part of a storage tank leak test. CATL acknowledged its contractor had acted “improperly” by discharging it into the sewer system and said the company would be in “full compliance” with environmental regulations in the future. The action against Semcorp coincided with the launch of a police probe against BYD, which is suspected of illegally moving toxic soil from its construction site in the southern city of Szeged to an outside location. Environment Minister Laszlo Gajdos called it a “serious breach” of its environmental permit. BYD has denied wrongdoing. BYD this week signed Orban’s former foreign minister, Peter Szijjarto, as its new global head of external relations, a move that ruffled feathers with the Magyar administration. Szijjarto had been the point-person in bringing EV investments to Hungary and had channeled hundreds of millions of dollars in state subsidies to them, including to BYD. He’s also facing a probe over his ties to the Kremlin. “It’s now clear for everyone why he lobbied for Chinese car and battery makers, sacrificing Hungarian water and risking the health of Hungarians,” Magyar said on Wednesday. The newfound scrutiny is being noticed in China. One China-based adviser, who has organized investments tours to Hungary for Chinese businesses in the past, canceled a planned trip after Debrecen’s mayor called on polluting companies to leave Hungary. The person, who asked not be identified, said Chinese clients now saw heightened risks in investing in Hungary. That’s not the new government’s aim, said Vitezy, the transportation minister, who said the goal was to maintain Chinese ties while respecting local and European rules and regulations. Besides EV investments, Hungary is currently finishing work on the Belgrade-Budapest rail line that’s part of China’s global infrastructure Belt and Road Initiative. Since Vitezy took office in May, contractors led by state-owned China Railway Engineering Corporation have been retrofitting the line with European-standard signaling systems so that it can legally carry passengers in addition to freight. Vitezy praised the speed of the Chinese partners, saying it took them “half the time” it would’ve taken a European company to do, which he said raised questions about the competitiveness of European rail companies. When it comes to EVs, he said the government is aware that Chinese battery and car makers chose Hungary not only because of Orban’s backing but because of the country’s already robust vehicle industry. That eco-system in Hungary includes BMW AG, Mercedes-Benz AG and Volkswagen AG, as well as Suzuki Corp. which all have major factories in Hungary. Magyar this week inaugurated the expansion of Mercedes’s plant in the central city of Kecskemet, which company Chief Executive Officer Ola Kaellenius called a “benchmark in Europe.” “The fact is we have a strong economic alliance between China and the Hungarian economy, given its reliance on the car industry generally,” Vitezy said. “Many of those Chinese batteries are going into German cars.” Bloomberg first published: Jul 18, 2026 03:47 pm Discover the latest Business News , Sensex , and Nifty updates. https://www.dumbartonreporter.co.uk/news.text: Ryanair warns of long EES queues at 16 European airports Entry Exit System Ryanair Leisure Travel By Patrick Glover Trending News Reporter Share 0 Comments The EU's Entry/Exit System (EES) continues to cause disruptions. (Image: Getty Images) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Ryanair has warned Brits travelling to Europe this summer to expect "significant" queues at 16 major airports. The warning comes as the European Union 's Entry/Exit System (EES) continues to create disruptions, months after its introduction. The EES was first introduced in October last year, before the rollout ramped up on April 10. The new system requires British travellers and other non-EU visitors to provide biometric data, including fingerprints and facial scans, when entering the Schengen Area. The new EES has received significant backlash since its introduction, with it causing long waits for passengers at airports. Some travellers have already experienced waits of up to six hours, and industry experts warn these disruptions could continue for up to two years . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Portugal Travel Advisor | Julia T (@travel_luckk) Major airlines, including Jet2 and Ryanair, have called for the rollout of the new system to be suspended until after the summer to allow for a "smoother airport experience" during peak travel season. CEO of Malta Air, David O’Brien, even threatened to pull all flights to Malta due to the extended wait times caused by the EES at airports. EES to cause long queues at these 16 major airports this summer Brits heading to Europe this summer have been told to expect more delays due to the EES. Ryanair has outlined 16 European Airports where travellers can expect "significant" queues: Tenerife South Palma/Majorca Alicante Malaga Milan Bergamo Krakow Paris Beauvais Lisbon Madrid Lanzarote Milan Malpensa Verona Berlin Cologne Frankfurt Hahn Budapest Chief operations officer at Ryanair, Neal McMahon, said: "Families heading away for a well-earned summer holiday should be thinking about suitcases, suncream and sangria, not standing in passport queues for hours. "The reality is that the EES system isn’t working properly and families are paying the price for a system that does not work months after launch. "Passengers should not be the testing ground for unfished border infrastructure." Mr McMahon has backed calls from EU Member States to extend current EES flexibilities into early 2027. This extension would give airports and border authorities more time to fix malfunctioning kiosks, increase staffing levels, and ensure the system can operate efficiently before full enforcement is introduced. He said: "We support calls from EU Member States to urgently extend the EES flexibilities. "This will give airports and border authorities the time to improve the infrastructure, fix the broken devices and hire more staff so that families can travel through Europe without disruption." Ryanair has advised UK passengers travelling to and from non-Schengen destinations, or transiting through affected European airports, to allow extra time for their journey and be prepared for lengthy waits at passport control. ETIAS launch delayed until 2027 Meanwhile, the launch of the EU's new European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS) has been delayed until 2027 . The ETIAS is a pre-authorisation scheme which will apply to UK passport holders and other visa-exempt travellers entering 30 European countries for short stays. Applicants will be required to pay a €20 fee, though travellers under 18 or over 70 will be exempt. The ETIAS was expected to launch later this year, but it has now been delayed until 2027, according to the Financial Times . The decision is due to "technical glitches" and delays with the EES, which only recently came online after being postponed from 2022. EU home affairs commissioner, Magnus Brunner, said the delays were due to "other factors", including insufficient staff or lack of adequate infrastructure. EU-Lisa, the agency responsible for ETIAS, has reportedly acknowledged that "launching it by the end of this year as planned was no longer feasible". The European Commission will set the official launch date only after EU-Lisa confirms the system has been fully tested and is ready. https://www.arbuturian.com/travel/travel.text: Trending Getting High in Haute-Savoie A Lunch with…Matthew Jukes Willett’s Nirvana Mediterranean Excellence: Reframing the All-Inclusive Up on the Hill: A Night Beneath the Chiltern Stars Roast in Peace: A Sunday at The Mutton Richard Dadd: A Much-Respected Murderer El Fuerte: Marbella’s Grand Dame, Reimagined Cooper’s Cut Ariadne auf Naxos at Glyndebourne M.C.Escher: The Exhibition Spa of the Month: Bellevue, Lošinj By Toby 'Lawrence' White on July 18, 2026 Travel In a distant corner of the Adriatic, once the Habsburgs’ cure for what ailed them, Larry checks into the boutique Hotel Alhambra, on an island that got there before wellness was a word… Technically, we’re in Istria. It’s a misty drive through pine-dressed mountains, terracotta rooftops, villages in various states of restoration and repose, and glimpses down to the sea. Losinj itself is something of a schlep, from anywhere, but I’ve written many a tome in these pages about the pleasure being in the journey, and the joys of losing yourself in a distant, discoverable part of the world. From Pula, we get our first glimpse of the destination as we round the top of the mainland, down to the ferry that carries us across to the islands. Once over the strait, it’s an hour down the length of Cres, the mountains taper into rolling heathland, through villages like Osor, from which we cross the smallest of bridges onto Losinj itself. We’re headed to Čikat Bay, a small cove on the far side of a narrow isthmus shaping a long natural harbour into Mali Losinj, the island’s largest town — though that rather overstates it. Here, cradled in pine woodland at the water’s edge, sits Hotel Alhambra; three buildings, two of them former villas — the oldest dating to 1908 — bookending a more contemporary addition. It’s part of a wider estate, Losinj Hotels & Villas, arranged around the bay to take in the sleeker Bellevue and five fin-de-siècle villas besides. With a scattering of independent cafés, eateries and activity outfits along the waterfront, it has all the benefits of a resort, just without the whiff of entrapment. Looking at this setting, I’m intrigued as to how these grand, palatial houses — now fitted out with mind-bogglingly stunning interiors — ever came to be here, in this distant, even remote corner of Croatia. The answer would come the next morning. For now, I was happy enough simply settling into this slice of idyll. Inside, the design is contemporary and eclectic, without losing its sense of history; stylised artworks show the villas in yesteryear, butting against striking modern fixtures, captured against the backdrop of the buildings’ original features. One minute you can be looking onto the bay through wraparound floor-to-ceiling windows in the lobby, then you turn a corner and enter the wood-panelled library, enjoying petit fours, served every tea time. My room is in one of the older buildings, so it keeps a number of original features. Perhaps the most striking touch, besides the double-height ceiling, is a bathroom that opens straight onto the terrace. There are lovely details, too; the motion sensor light in the walk-in wardrobe, the mood lighting, the TV speakers built into the bathroom mirror — useful when not wishing to miss the news while preparing for dinner. That evening, at Alfred Keller, Alhambra’s Michelin-starred restaurant, I crack the wax seal on a menu billed as three courses that amounts to nearer eight. I’m not sure why I should be surprised to find exceptional cuisine tucked into a secluded cove on this distant stretch of the Adriatic — Michelin reaches most corners of the world these days — but I was. Snacks alongside a Slavonian barrel-aged negroni ran to a parmesan and truffle croquette, presented as a black truffle on a bed of moss, and bacon-wrapped asparagus with goat’s cheese foam. The highlight, though, was the kingfish — flambéed, the waiter told me, a technique I thought had gone out with the ’70s — in a tangy tomato consommé with pickled fennel. There are joys, too, among the wines. A sparkling Tomac, rivalling anything southeast England might produce, would become a new regular aperitif on my visit. Being in such a pine-rich, picturesque setting rather infuses one with a desire to embrace nature. In my case, quite literally. The spa offers rituals of an arboreal bent, so, duly fortified with a hot ginger and lemon before breakfast, I’m out into the woods for a mindful ‘breathing’ session among the trees. A shoreline promenade runs not just around Čikat Bay but much of the island, and it’s here, walking through the pines with the sea lapping just feet away, that you get a real sense of place. It is, entirely, serene. I pass jasmine and am awash with scent. The island’s restorative reputation, it turns out, is not just hokum. On this meandering walk I learn why the villas exist here at all. Under the Austro-Hungarian empire, Losinj became known as a health resort, thanks largely to the botanist Ambroz Haračić — commemorated with a statue in the bay — who catalogued the island’s flora while searching for a cure for his son’s asthma. Word spread, and soon the Habsburgs’ glitterati were building palatial holiday homes in this botanically rich corner of the empire. A handful of those properties have since become Alhambra and its villas, and staying in them, I confess to feeling ever so slightly imperious myself, lordly parading down to the seafront in my bathrobe. Even today, with 1,200 plant species and its agreeable climate, Losinj ranks among the most botanically wealthy islands in the Mediterranean, a legacy the hotel’s spa captures with an “inhalation bar” — its take on a respiratory tonic that dates to 1892, when aristocratic visitors would stop at the island’s Kurhaus to breathe in mists of seawater and medicinal aerosols. Waiting for my therapist and a signature herbal massage, I find the modern equivalent: an antique cabinet housing a bulbous ceramic vessel from which one inhales plant-infused sea air. Perhaps more psychosomatic than efficacious, but between the botanical walk, the cold sea plunges from the sundecks and a lungful of resin-scented air at every turn, I was beginning to feel thoroughly, if implausibly, cured. It wouldn’t be Croatia without getting out on the water, and this being a lesser-known region, there are some genuinely untapped spots left to find. Sailing might be the purist’s choice, but without the luxury of time, a powerboat — sun deck, naturally — is the more efficient option. We skip across to Susak, visible from Losinj, for a spot of exploratory beachcombing. It has a population today of barely 150 — a small port village, a church and a lighthouse marking its highest points — and crossing the water towards it feels rather like crossing time. Before the war, the population was closer to 1,600, ten times its current size, and the island lived on wine; when the new communist government taxed the trade into oblivion, the islanders left, most of them for Hoboken, New Jersey. But, remarkably, their descendants still return every summer. More developed is Ilovik, tucked into Losinj’s tail and known as the ‘Island of Flowers’ for its own abundance of oleander, rose and eucalyptus. Heading back up the coast to Mali Losinj, I find it remarkable that a stretch of the Mediterranean this handsome hasn’t been given over to wall-to-wall hotels. What stays with me most is the colour of the water — the Adriatic has a shade of blue entirely its own. A hundred yards up the promenade, in some contrast to Alhambra, sits the larger, more contemporary Bellevue. Here, in the spirit of the sea’s bounty, we dine at Matsunoki, the group’s award-laden Japanese restaurant. After a run of tasting starters — Kobe beef fukuju, beef tataki with truffle mayonnaise, duck gyoza, tuna tartare — comes a sashimi course of remarkable range: sea bass, a volcano tuna roll, golden dragon, wagyu asparagus, plus salmon, hamachi and tuna sashimi, alongside an exquisite 40%-polished Fukujo ‘blue’ sake. Ironically, for all that dazzling fish, the highlight turns out to be the simplicity of a miso ice cream for dessert, even upstaging the strudel-like apple gyoza it accompanies. It’s hard to leave Alhambra without feeling that the whole place is, in some sense, still practising what those nineteenth-century botanists preached. The pines that shelter it, the sea that laps at its jetty, the very air one is encouraged to breathe more deeply — none of it is incidental; it’s the point, and has been for well over a century. Other hotels borrow the language of wellness. Alhambra simply inherited it, along with the villas, the woodland and the view. A heritage of healing, a legacy of luxury, as they put it themselves — and, for once, the strapline undersells it. I came in search of nothing more than a good story and a decent dinner. I left rather wondering whether I’d been cured of something I hadn’t known was wrong with me. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/becomes-i.text: Jon Henley Europe correspondent Updated Sat, 18 July 2026 at 4:20 pm UTC 18 The long-time politician Ann Widdecombe was found dead in her home in Devon, England, last week.Photograph: Jack Taylor/Reuters On 9 July, the body of Ann Widdecombe, an uncompromising, staunchly conservative former UK government minister turned TV personality and spokesperson for the radical-right Reform UK party, was found at her home in south-west England. Two days later, a man was arrested in South Yorkshire. Believed to be previously unknown to the local police force and thought to have acted alone, he is suspected of driving 270 miles (435km) to the 78-year-old politician’s home and causing her catastrophic blunt-force injuries. Police have been examining whether a leftwing or single-issue cause may lie behind her killing. Ten years after the murder of the Labour MP Jo Cox by a far-right extremist , five years after a Conservative MP, David Amess, was stabbed to death by a supporter of Islamic State, and as MPs from across the political spectrum report a tide of abuse and threats, the killing has reignited the UK’s debate on political violence. Attacks against elected officials across the political spectrum are rising not just in Britain but across the west, with experts saying that ever more dehumanising rhetoric, declining institutional trust and widespread disinformation are combining to create a growing problem. Five years ago, in 2021, police in the US recorded more than 9,600 threats against members of Congress. The following year, the husband of the former House speaker Nancy Pelosi was attacked with a hammer by a rightwing conspiracy theorist. Also in 2022, a New York gubernatorial candidate, Lee Zeldin, was attacked with a sharp object . Two years later, in 2024, Donald Trump faced two assassination attempts, including one in Butler county, Pennsylvania, in which a bullet grazed his ear . Last year, the home of the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, was firebombed; a gunman dressed as a police officer killed a Minnesota lawmaker and her husband and badly wounded another and his wife; and the far-right youth figurehead Charlie Kirk was shot dead . In continental Europe, Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, was shot multiple times by a 71-year-old man while greeting supporters in Handlová, about 90 miles north-east of the capital, Bratislava, in May 2024. He survived after life-saving surgery. The following month, the Danish prime minister, Mette Fredriksen, was assaulted while walking through a square in central Copenhagen. She suffered minor head, neck and shoulder injuries but said the psychological shock had affected her most. High-profile leaders are not the only targets. Germany recorded 5,140 politically motivated offences against politicians in 2025, almost double the 2023 figure of 2,790. An MEP , a senator and a far-right Alternative für Deutschland candidate were among the victims. The same trend is evident in France. An interior ministry unit that monitors attacks on elected officials recorded about 2,500 incidents in 2025 but more than 1,500 in the first five months of 2026 alone, with local mayors accounting for 64% of victims. Most of the incidents in France (about 65%) involved death threats and verbal abuse. About 10% involve property damage and a similar percentage physical violence: in May, one local mayor needed hospital treatment after an attack over a housing request. According to the conflict monitoring group Acled , violence and intimidatory acts targeting local officials in particular jumped by 46% across Europe from 2024 to 2025, with the highest proportion of serious incidents recorded in Italy. Experts have argued that increasingly violent rhetoric that routinely demonises political opponents is clearly a factor: when public figures are framed not just as wrong but as “traitors” or “enemies”, radicalised individuals may feel freer to act. In a recent analysis , the academics Andrea Ruggeri, Ursula Daxecker and Neeraj Prasad said violence risked becoming “part of the political process” because of a “toxic mix of elite rhetoric, weakened party structures and spiralling polarisation”. When leaders “normalise hostility”, influencers “amplify fear” and parties “outsource mobilisation to extremists”, argued the authors, from the universities of Milan and Amsterdam, “political violence ceases to be unthinkable and becomes inevitable”. Law enforcement officials stress that the structure of political violence is shifting. In the past, the main threat in the US and Europe was from organised extremist groups, they said, while perpetrators were now more likely to be isolated lone actors. “While jihadist terrorism continues to constitute the most persistent threat, the lines between established terrorist ideologies and other forms of violent extremism are becoming increasingly blurred,” said Europol’s most recent TE-SAT terrorism report . Modern attackers tend to be radicalised in “nihilistic” digital communities where violence is “gamified” and marked by an “ideological fluidity” that often combines conspiracy theories, anti-system narratives and personal grievance. Where one ideology is dominant, it produces “single-issue extremism”, typically associated with highly emotive topics such as extreme rightwing xenophobia, anti-state sentiment, anti-vaccination conviction, environmental radicalism or “Incel” beliefs. But common to many lone actors, Europol says, is a deep-seated hostility towards “the establishment”, state authority and the democratic process – making mayors, MPs and ministers targets not just for their policies but as symbols of the system. Because these individuals act independently, they do not generate the kind of communications or logistical footprint that security agencies typically intercept, making it hugely difficult for police to detect and prevent attacks on politicians. That, in turn, has brought into sharper focus the question of security arrangements for politicians. In the UK, the Reform party, led by Nigel Farage, has been widely accused of exploiting Widdecombe’s death to claim its MPs are not protected enough. The fact that the radical-right party itself has rarely shied away from the kind of inflammatory rhetoric seen as at least partially responsible for the recent surge in political violence has not escaped Reform’s opponents – but the issue is a live one. Like most countries, the UK has increased security for politicians in recent years. As in the US and many European countries, senior ministers have security details, but individual members of parliament do not unless they face a specific threat. The same is true of countries such as France and Germany, both of which have recently established networks linking local police forces to MPs’ constituency offices and increased penalties for acts of violence against elected officials. The former German justice minister Nancy Faeser described the trend as “an escalation of democratic contempt” that was “increasingly turning into physical violence”, and demanded that perpetrators felt “the full force of the law”. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP Spain At least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco Pedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incident Sam Jones in Madrid, Angela Giuffrida in Rome and Jakub Krupa Fri 31 Jul 2026 13.52 EDT First published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 03.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 50,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , called “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”. The huge influx, which took place over the course of just 24 hours, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to a mixed reaction from other EU countries, including calls for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. 3:37 Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spanish enclave Ceuta from Morocco - video Sánchez, who arrived in Ceuta on Friday morning, said he would use all the resources at his disposal to guarantee the safety of the city’s population. He attributed the mass crossing to “human trafficking mafias” that had taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta, or Spain’s other north African enclave of Melilla, could not be summarily returned under special rules. Sánchez said: “That has spread like wildfire during these last few hours through the networks of mafias that traffic in human beings and has produced an avalanche of the characteristics and dimension that we experienced yesterday.” Sánchez said a temporary reception centre would be established to facilitate the documentation, registration, triage and “expedited” expulsion of people with no legal claim to be in Spain. Hundreds of migrants run and cheer as they enter Spain’s enclave of Ceuta He also said the government would erect a visible barrier – a line of buoys – near the breakwater at Ceuta’s Tarajal beach to make it clear where the border was, and to legally comply with the court’s ruling. Although the Spanish government said about 50,000 people had crossed the border on Thursday and in the early hours of Friday, the president of Ceuta put the figure at about 60,000. Spain’s interior ministry, which has deployed additional police officers and soldiers to the enclave, said more than 48,300 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco by 6pm on Friday. The Irish presidency of the EU has convened a meeting of member states on Saturday, under the Integrated Political Crisis Response mechanism. EU sources said this will provide experts from member states with an opportunity “to discuss the movements into Ceuta over the last two days, the numbers of people who have returned to Morocco today, the supports being provided by the EU to Spain and diplomatic engagement with Morocco”. A further meeting of EU ambassadors has been called in Brussels on Monday. The latest incident dwarfs the last mass border crossing in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over the course of two days. Map showing location of Ceuta between Spain and Morocco, and another map showing location of Tarajal breakwater in Ceuta That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania. That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara – a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group. Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria. Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”. Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich, was quoted by the Associated Press as saying that “we have always prioritized legal, orderly and safe migration for all” and indicated that the situation had developed against Rabat’s wishes. View image in fullscreen Spain’s interior ministry said more than 48,300 people decided to return to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Friday. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers’ association representing officers of the Spanish Guardia Civil – which patrols Spain’s borders – described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”. Without shelter, thousands of people, including unaccompanied children, had been left sleeping in parks and on pavements, while others roamed the streets aimlessly. “It’s chaotic,” said Sbihi. Among those who died, many drowned, but some were killed in a crush to cross the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach, Sbihi said. View image in fullscreen People waiting on the Moroccan side of the border for a chance to cross to Ceuta. Photograph: Reuters Video footage on Thursday showed crowds of people walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach on to local roads. While most appeared to be young men, there were also families with women and small children. Ceuta and Melilla have the E​U’s only land border with ​Africa. ‌Both cities ​periodically ​experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to reach Europe . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Crowds in downtown Ceuta on Friday after making the crossing. Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/Reuters The events in Ceuta led some EU countries to issue strong threats or rebukes. Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, summoned Italy’s ambassador to Madrid on Friday after Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now closed scheme to regularise the status of more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”. Tajani’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Albares, who said the comments were “unbecoming” and accused Italy of “partisan demagoguery”. Italy announced on Friday evening that it would be suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain, but the practical impact of the move was not immediately clear. Meloni said the measure would be kept in force only as long as needed, adding: “In parallel, Italy is ready to support every European initiative to assist Spanish institutions as needed to restore full control of the union’s external borders and to address the ongoing situation with determination.” View image in fullscreen Spanish soldiers patrolling the Spanish-Moroccan border in Ceuta on Friday. Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/Reuters Responding to Italy’s unilateral decision, a European Commission spokesperson said a member state “may exceptionally and temporarily reintroduce internal border control as a matter of last resort, to address serious threats to public order or national security”. But they added that the member state would need to notify the commission and explain how the situation in Ceuta constituted such a threat. The Guardian understands that Italy has not yet formally notified any of its EU partners of its decision. The Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, urged Spain to “act swiftly to regain control of the situation and fulfil its commitments within Schengen cooperation”. The Finnish interior minister, Mari Rantanen, said that as Spain had “completely failed to protect the Schengen area’s external border”, all EU countries should support Italy’s proposal to suspend its Schengen status. However, in a statement later on Friday, the European Commission said Ceuta and Melilla were subject to special Schengen rules that prevented onward movement within the zone. View image in fullscreen Belongings float in the sea after they were left behind by people crossing from Morocco into Ceuta. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP The EU’s migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, called the situation in Ceuta “unacceptable” and said he was in close contact with the Spanish authorities. But he also confirmed there was no onward route from Ceuta given the enclave’s unique status under the Schengen rules. He said: “The Schengen borders code provides for special rules that apply to Ceuta and Melilla. Border checks on persons departing from Ceuta and Melilla remain in force.” But there were also shows of unity. The European Council president, António Costa, expressed his “solidarity with Spain in the current situation of illegal migration in Ceuta”. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had been in touch with the Spanish government to express his solidarity and to offer assistance to Spain. But, as a precautionary measure, Macron said he had asked the interior ministry to strengthen the French controls on its border with Spain with four mobile units and drones. In Spain, the opposition People’s party (PP) called on Sánchez to come up with a tough response, saying the military and police reinforcements announced on Thursday night were insufficient. In a post on X, the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, wrote: “People have continued to arrive in Ceuta throughout the night, and those on the ground describe an occupied city, with nothing sufficient being done to prevent it.” The far-right Vox party called the incident “an invasion”. On Friday evening, hundreds attended an anti-migrant rally outside the Moroccan embassy in Madrid, with images showing some protesters performing Nazi salutes and waving flags with far-right insignia. There have been 3,360 confirmed cases of the virus in the east of the country. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/EPA Global development Ebola outbreak in DRC the fastest growing in the history of the virus As the death toll rises to almost 1,500, and with a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain potentially still months away, health workers face a battle to slow the outbreak Supported by About this content Prosper Heri Ngorora in Bunia Fri 31 Jul 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 04.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The latest numbers of confirmed cases of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has made this latest outbreak the fastest growing in the known history of the virus. At 3,360 confirmed cases , the disease is now affecting people in five provinces in the east of the DRC, with 1,487 deaths recorded, representing an overall case fatality rate estimated at about 45%, according to Congolese health officials. Health responses to the outbreak have been badly hampered by conflict in many of the affected areas. “I fear that at some point, life may come to a standstill here in our province of Ituri,” said Deborah Nzuva, a mother of four who lives in Rwampara, one of the affected regions. “We were already in a precarious situation before the Ebola virus disease, which continues to claim its victims.” Since officially declared by the Congolese authorities on 15 May, the Bundibugyo strain of the virus has spread faster than any of the country’s 16 previous Ebola outbreaks – and the numbers are approaching the previous worst toll, in 2018-2020 when 3,470 people in DRC were infected. Prof Pierre Akilimali, from the country’s public health institute (NPHI), is in charge of the Ebola response. He emphasises that the disease continues to spread and that it is still difficult to know when it will reach its peak. According to him, there is a way to go and the road to bringing the outbreak under control is a long one. View image in fullscreen Members of a Congolese Red Cross team in Bunia carry the body of a woman suspected of having died from Ebola, 7 June. Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty Images “Here in Ituri, we have the issues of insecurity, mining and high population density, which make the current outbreak more complex than previous ones,” he said. The Congolese authorities say they have taken a number of measures to limit spread, including strengthening surveillance through community liaison officers, building more than 20 Ebola treatment centres, and setting up local laboratories for testing. “The public must also play their part by seeking medical advice at the slightest suspicion of infection,” Akilimali said. “This will help us to respond effectively to the disease.” He said cases continue to rise in the Bunia and Rwampara health zones, with between 100 and 150 new confirmed infections each week. Annabelle Nissi, a clothing trader in Bunia, said people were living in fear. “This outbreak is causing us great distress. Our hope lies solely in God’s hands. It continues to disrupt our lives and has brought our development projects to a standstill,” she said. Dr Justus Nsio, field incident manager for the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said it was a race against time. First patients enrolled in record-breaking Ebola treatment trial in DRC Read more “All the experts monitoring this outbreak agree that it was detected too late. When detection is delayed, we have to work hard to make up for what we missed earlier in order to contain the disease,” he said. “What is certain is that, with the commitment of the movement and our partners, the outcome will be favourable.” View image in fullscreen Health workers prepare for a safe burial operation in the community of Mongbwalu, Ituri, DRC, in May. Photograph: Michel Lunanga/Getty Images Clinical trials began in early July of a vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no standard treatment. As of 15 July, about 20 people had been enrolled in these trials, which could last up to four months, according to Prof Placide Mbala, head of laboratory operations for the Ebola response in the DRC. Uganda, which this week declared the Ebola outbreak over on its territory, 12 days after its last case was reported, has sent experts to the DRC to work alongside their Congolese counterparts, particularly in the border regions of Tchomia and Kasenyi. Photograph: Cole Burston/AFP/Getty Images Wildfires Past fires suggest effects of Europe and North America wildfires may linger for years Three years after Maui wildfires many still struggle with ‘biological, emotional and social consequences’, study says Oliver Milman Tue 28 Jul 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 00.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A spate of ferocious wildfires across North America and Europe , worsened by the climate crisis, has incinerated homes and forests and forced thousands of people to flee. Previous fires suggest the effects of these blazes may linger for years to come. The current fires and their plumes of smoke can appear to be a temporary, if immediate, crisis. Nearly 1,000 fires have sprung into life in the boreal forests of Canada, causing the evacuation of towns and toxic smoke to waft into major Canadian and US cities, prompting threats of retribution from Donald Trump, who bizarrely accused Canada of “poisoning” his country’s air. Smoke is billowing from wildfires in the US too, amid the third major heatwave of the past month which has furthered dried out parched vegetation. Vast, lightning-sparked fires across Washington, eastern Oregon and Idaho have caused a plume of smoke so large that it could reach Florida. In Europe, meanwhile, huge fires have gripped parts of the UK , France and Spain , causing the evacuation of more than 250,000 people. View image in fullscreen A house damaged by wildfires in Blagon, south-western France, on Monday. Photograph: Laurent Perpigna/EPA The climate crisis, caused by the burning of fossil fuels, is known to be creating more fire-prone conditions around the world by drying out soils and plants. “The entire Iberian peninsula is suffering the effects of the climate emergency in a very specific way,” said Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s prime minister. Scientists have also long been aware of the unhealthy consequences of wildfire smoke, which can trigger severe respiratory and cardiac problems in affected people. A recent study found that exposure to tiny particles carried in wildfire smoke will raise the risk of hospitalization for older people hundreds of miles away from fires. “The cardiovascular toll of wildfire smoke reaches well beyond the fire lines and well beyond the day the sky turns orange,” said Kai Chen, associate professor of epidemiology at the Yale School of Public Health and study co-author. But identifying the ongoing effects of wildfires long after they have been extinguished has been a more recent understanding. There are continuing challenges in Maui, the second largest of Hawaii’s islands, three years after wildfires there caused more than 100 deaths and razed several thousand buildings, a new report highlights. While living and economic conditions have generally improved since the fires, many people in Maui are still struggling with health concerns such as poorer lung functions, higher blood pressure and mental health challenges, according to the Maui Wildfire Exposure Study , led by researchers at the University of Hawaii and released on Monday. View image in fullscreen An aerial view of vegetation regrowth amid areas destroyed or damaged by the Lahaina wildfire, including the iconic banyan tree, on 4 August 2024 in Lahaina, Hawaii. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images “The progress is real, and it should be recognized,” said Alika Maunakea, co-director of the study and a school of medicine professor at the University of Hawaii. “But the biological, emotional and social consequences of a disaster do not disappear on the same timeline as debris removal or reconstruction.” Nearly half of all adults in the Maui study continued to report depressive symptoms, with nearly one in five experiencing post-traumatic stress. The study, which conducted screenings of more than 2,500 participants, also found severe depressive symptoms and post-traumatic stress increased among children and adolescents, as did blood pressure readings and obesity levels. “Children may appear resilient while still carrying significant emotional and physical effects beneath the surface,” said Christopher Knightsbridge, a mental health therapist based in Lahaina, a coastal town that was largely destroyed by the fires. “Supporting children means supporting the entire family, including their housing, food security, daily routines and access to trusted care,” he added. The researchers stressed that long-term monitoring and intervention is required following a major wildfire event due to impacts that can last for years afterwards. While the skies over North America and Europe will eventually clear of smoke after a tinderbox summer of fire, this climate change-driven era of wildfire is set to exact a lengthy toll. As well as better support for those directly affected by fires, experts say that authorities in smoke-affected areas could respond to the threat of repeated smoke exposure by creating “clean air centers” that people can flee to in order to escape smoke and other air pollutants. A research paper from last year , which found a 7% increase in mortality among a cohort of older people living in southern California over a three-year period due to wildfire smoke exposure, recommended that “activation of public health measures such as clean air centers should not only depend on intensity of smoke, as the long-term effects can be harmful, even at low levels.” Lara Schwarz, an environmental health scientist at UC Berkley who led the research, said: “As wildfires become more frequent and severe in the context of climate change, with California being at high risk, understanding how these harmful wildfires will affect us in the long term is critical to informing better public health action and response.” Explore more on these topics Wildfires France Canada Americas Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Daughter of British couple killed in Spanish wildfire rejects claim they ignored order to leave Europe burns: a visual guide to the wildfires ‘Extremely scary findings’ show climate crisis is supercharging Europe’s wildfire weather ‘We can’t make it better again’: what Europe’s wildfires tell us about the climate crisis Wildfire near Sizewell nuclear plant causes ‘total devastation’ to Suffolk landscape Race to extinguish blazes across Europe as fire weather breaks records Will brutal wildfires force French leaders to take climate crisis seriously? Photograph: Fundacion Victor Jara, Antonio L/AP Chile Pinochet-era soldier jailed for killing folk singer Víctor Jara 53 years ago Nelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in Chile John Bartlett in Santiago Mon 27 Jul 2026 12.27 EDT Last modified on Tue 28 Jul 2026 05.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 50 years after the murder of the Chilean folk singer Víctor Jara , the last man wanted in connection with his death has been tracked down and brought to justice. Nelson Haase Mazzei, a retired colonel, fled from authorities in 2023 after he and six other retired soldiers were sentenced in absentia for murdering Jara and another man. Chilean police announced on Saturday that Haase Mazzei had been arrested in Puyehue, in the rural south of the country, with a judge ordering his immediate imprisonment. The Víctor Jara Foundation, set up by his widow, the British dancer and activist Joan Jara, said in statement: “We learned that retired Colonel Nelson Haase Mazzei, who had been a fugitive from justice since 2023, was found and imprisoned. We welcome this news. “However, it is important for us to emphasize that, half a century after the murders of Víctor Jara and Littré Quiroga, it is difficult to see this as this justice.” Jara, a singer and leftwing activist, was detained in Santiago, the capital of Chile, on 12 September 1973, the day after Gen Augusto Pinochet’s bloody US-backed coup to depose the socialist president, Salvador Allende. View image in fullscreen Víctor Jara’s widow, Joan, who died in 2023, was a British dancer and activist who set up a foundation in her late husband’s name. Photograph: Roberto Candia/AP Jara was held along with thousands of others at a small covered stadium in central Santiago. Four days later, he was murdered in the changing rooms alongside Allende’s national director of prisons, Littré Quiroga. Haase Mazzei’s arrest is likely to be the final act in the long quest for justice on behalf of Jara, one of the most recognisable victims of the Pinochet dictatorship, which killed or disappeared more than 3,000 people and detained and tortured tens of thousands during 17 years of repressive rule. At the stadium, Jara was tortured and humiliated by officers who played Russian roulette with him before breaking his hands, shattering his skull, and riddling him with automatic gunfire. His body was found dumped near the main cemetery in Santiago with 44 bullet wounds and 56 broken bones. He was 40 years old. The body of Quiroga, who had been shot 23 times, was found at the same time. After evading justice for nearly half a century, seven retired soldiers were found guilty of the murder and sentenced in absentia to varying jail terms in August 2023. Haase Mazzei received a 25-year sentence. He claimed for years that he was not at the stadium, since renamed Estadio Víctor Jara, but sworn testimony placed him at the scene. Haase Mazzei joined the Chilean army’s notorious Tejas Verde brigade in 1972, and was later part of Pinochet’s secret police, the Dirección Nacional de Inteligencia (Dina), where he worked closely with its leader, Manuel Contreras, a renowned regime loyalist who was sentenced to more than 500 years’ jail time for crimes against humanity before his death in 2015. View image in fullscreen Pedro Barrientos being deported from the US to Chile in 2023. Photograph: Policia de Investigaciones de Chile/Reuters Sentenced alongside Haase Mazzei was 86-year-old Hernán Chacón. When police arrived to arrest him at his home in a wealthy district of Santiago in 2023, he asked officers for a moment to take his medication, before slipping off into a side room and taking his own life. Another Tejas Verde officer sentenced for the killing was Pedro Barrientos, who left Chile for the US in 1989 and was deported back in December 2023 , more than a decade after his extradition was first sought. One former soldier testified that Barrientos had the habit of brandishing his pistol and declaring: “I killed Víctor Jara with this!” Barrientos was eventually arrested in the US after a routine traffic stop, and lost his US citizenship not because of his crimes, but on the grounds that he had failed to disclose his military background in his application. Jara’s widow died at the age of 96, just weeks before Barrientos was returned to Chile to face justice. Haase Mazzei’s defence has already requested his transfer from a prison in the southern city of Osorno to Punta Peuco, a well-appointed jail north of Santiago, built to house the human rights criminals of the Pinochet era. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/j.text: 0:43 Police footage shows scale of damage inside Aeon mall after explosion cause by Japan quake – video Japan Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 30 as aftershock and heat hamper rescue efforts Soldiers and emergency teams search damaged shopping centre, paper mill and homes for survivors Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in pictures Gavin Blair in Tokyo Thu 30 Jul 2026 02.49 EDT First published on Wed 29 Jul 2026 22.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The death toll from the powerful earthquake that hit Japan on Tuesday has risen to 30, as the search for survivors trapped in a badly damaged shopping centre, paper mill and collapsed homes across the south-west of the country continues. ‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquake Read more The 6.8-magnitude quake, which struck Kumamoto prefecture on the island of Kyushu, injured at least 62 people, according to the prefectural government. Almost 5,000 Self-Defence Forces (SDF) personnel deployed to the region faced temperatures of up to 35C on Thursday, officials said, adding that a 5.8-magnitude aftershock overnight had further hampered the rescue efforts. Map of earthquake site About 170 rescue workers were searching the Aeon shopping centre in the town of Kashima, which was bustling with thousands of people when the quake struck. The company said about 3,000 customers were evacuated to a car park before a gas explosion occurred in another part of the shopping centre. Six of the 12 people pulled from the rubble have died. All those caught in the explosion were shop workers who had returned to the building after the evacuation, Aeon said. The company’s president bowed in apology at a press conference on Wednesday, saying Aeon had failed to anticipate the explosion, the cause of which was being investigated. 1:09 Aerial footage shows collapsed buildings after 6.8 magnitude Japan earthquake – video Japanese media footage from inside the shopping centre showed part of the ceiling had collapsed, with metal fragments and other debris scattered across the floor as helmeted, masked rescue workers searched the area. Police and SDF personnel were continuing to search for one worker in the debris at the Nippon Paper mill in Yatsushiro, where a chimney collapsed. Of the 10 others who were trapped, eight died and two were injured. In the first reported death of a foreign national, a Vietnamese technical intern was killed after a crane fell on him at the factory where he worked, according to the Vietnamese government. View image in fullscreen Nippon Paper mill, where a chimney collapsed. Photograph: Jiji Press/EPA Nearly 23,000 homes had no electricity and 75,000 had no running water, Kumamoto officials said. About 15,000 people had been evacuated to 400 shelters. The defence minister said on Wednesday evening that the SDF was airlifting coolers to shelters in Kumamoto, while SDF vessels were delivering water and food. “We’re doing everything possible to make saving lives a priority, making efforts to deliver life-saving supplies, beginning with water,” Shinjiro Koizumi said. Aerial police footage showed several homes had been flattened, including some that had crumbled into a river. View image in fullscreen A collapsed house in Hikawa, Kumamoto. Photograph: Kyodo/Reuters The earthquake registered the maximum level 7 on Japan’s seven-level shindo scale. “It was the strongest quake I have ever experienced,” Kanzo Matsumoto, 73, the operator of a luxury hot spring inn in Yatsushiro, told Agence France-Presse. The national Geospatial Information Authority said parts of the ground had shifted by 87cm during the quake. Yatsushiro town hall sustained damage to its base-isolation system, an earthquake-resistant technology designed to protect buildings by cushioning their foundations against intense shaking. The system was rebuilt after a deadly earthquake in 2016. View image in fullscreen Vehicles are crushed under collapsed buildings in Yatsushiro, south-western Japan. Photograph: Hiro Komae/AP Some car and semiconductor manufacturers with plants in Kyushu have halted production. Toyota said it would pause operations at three plants while it assessed the quake’s impact on suppliers and ⁠logistics. Honda suspended operations at a motorcycle plant until Friday. Taiwan’s TSMC has resumed operations at its Kumamoto facility, while Sony, Renesas Electronics and Tokyo Electron have halted production. Kyushu is ‌an important hub for Japan’s automotive and semiconductor industries, which account for about 20% of the region’s industrial output. Analysts said the shutdowns appeared to be driven largely by precaution than damage to production facilities. Kumamoto was struck by two devastating earthquakes in 2016 that killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.The archipelago, home to about 125 million people, usually experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18% of the world’s earthquakes. Photograph: Naoki Hiraoka/Kyodo News/AP Japan ‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquake Rescuers pulling people from the wreckage in southern Japan in a haunting repeat of disaster that struck 10 years ago ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing Gavin Blair in Tokyo Wed 29 Jul 2026 05.08 EDT Last modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 15.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “T here was a voice coming from the collapsed house, and I could see a hand,” Tomohide Nagata, a volunteer firefighter, told the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun. “One of our senior members crawled in and pulled him out. He was bleeding from the head, but I’m so glad he survived.” Nagata had heard a noise coming from one completely flattened home in the rural town of Hikawa, close to the epicentre of Tuesday’s 6.8-magnitude earthquake in southern Japan. The town was one of the areas hardest hit, with numerous older houses collapsing. Terrified of the ongoing aftershocks, many residents spent Tuesday night in their cars outside Hikawa’s town hall, where staff distributed food and drinks. ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing Read more At least 13 people were killed and hundreds injured when the earthquake struck the island of Kyushu. The prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said on Wednesday: “There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it’s a race against time. We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.” Iwaoka Shigemi, 79, and his wife, Michiyo, 77, had escaped from their house and spent the night sleeping in their car in Hikawa, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. With temperatures expected to reach 35C on Wednesday, they were now worried about the risk of heatstroke. Suemi Nagata, 79, was unable to escape Hikawa by car because her garage had been destroyed but had made it to the town hall with her husband and older sister. “The lateral shaking was worse than the Kumamoto earthquake 10 years ago, and it was terrifying,” she told the town’s local newspaper. “Just to have survived with my life is something to be grateful for.” View image in fullscreen A damaged road in Hikawa. Photograph: Kyodo/Reuters In April, the prefecture of Kumamoto commemorated the 10th anniversary of the 2016 earthquake that killed more than 275 people and caused widespread devastation. In that case, a 6.2-magnitude foreshock was followed two days later by the deadly 7-magnitude quake, something that will be on the mind of tens of thousands across Kumamoto in the week ahead. At the Kumamoto Aeon mall, which was severely damaged by what is understood to have been a gas explosion triggered by the earthquake, a number of employees had gone back inside after evacuating customers and were caught in the blast. A 16-year-old girl who got out with other shoppers moments before the explosion, told the Asahi Shimbun she “felt completely safe once she was outside”, only to be left struggling to breathe by dust and smoke. A 74-year-old man who often shopped at the mall told the Nikkei newspaper that he had just learned that an acquaintance who worked there was hurt. “I could have been caught up in it myself,” he said. Up to 30 employees were initially reported trapped inside and four remain missing. View image in fullscreen A rescue worker walks in front of the Aeon mall, which was damaged by an explosion after the earthquake. Photograph: Hiro Komae/AP In nearby Uki City, which also experienced shaking ranked at the maximum 7 on the Japanese shindo scale, residents told of lucky escapes and heartbreaking unsuccessful rescue efforts. Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in pictures Read more A woman in her 40s had managed to get to an evacuation shelter with three generations of her family after putting herself between falling furniture and her children. “I was pinned under a chest of drawers at home. I protected my children and then hurried to evacuate,” she told the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun from Toyono elementary school, which was being used as an evacuation shelter after the ceiling of the local disaster facility fell in. On Tuesday evening as neighbours and relatives attempted to check in on each other, residents in the Asakawa district of Uki found one house flattened, with roof tiles scattered on the ground around where it had once stood. As family members looked on, a handful of volunteer firefighters attempted to rescue an elderly man trapped inside. “The man is a childhood friend of mine,” the visibly shaken 70-year-old head of the local district told the Kumamoto newspaper. “We tried to pull him out, but the aftershocks came one after another, so we had no choice but to give up.” As in Hikawa, many Uki residents slept in their cars, and local government workers handed out water and food. Unable to use the damaged disaster facility, the city set up a makeshift response headquarters in a car park. In Yatsushiro, south of Hikawa, one man’s life may have been saved by his schedule when his workplace, a single-storey wooden structure, collapsed. “It was a day off and I wasn’t at work, so I escaped with my life,” said the self-employed man, 63, who spent the night in a tent pitched in his garden. “Though I have no idea what I’ll do starting tomorrow.” Explore more on these topics Japan Earthquakes Asia Pacific features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 30 as aftershock and heat hamper rescue efforts 'People are waiting to be rescued': race under way to find Japan quake survivors – video ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in pictures Dashcam captures moment 6.8-magnitude earthquake hits Japan – video Japan earthquake injures at least 100 and kills two inside shopping mall Aerial footage shows collapsed buildings after 6.8 magnitude Japan earthquake – video Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: imageBROKER/David & Micha Sheldon/Getty Images/imageBROKER RF View image in fullscreen More than 80 dead and dying greater crested terns have been spotted off the South Australian coast in what is a suspected H5N1 bird flu mass mortality event. Photograph: imageBROKER/David & Micha Sheldon/Getty Images/imageBROKER RF Bird flu First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds Helicopter surveillance finds dead and dying greater crested terns off South Australian coast as H5 virus spreads Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent Sat 1 Aug 2026 02.12 EDT Last modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 80 dead and sick birds seen on rocks off the South Australian coast are suspected to be the first mass mortality event from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, only six weeks after the disease arrived in Australia. Authorities reported on Saturday that helicopter surveillance had revealed 49 dead greater crested terns on Baudin Rocks, near Robe, as well as 35 more sick terns. While some of the birds had been collected for testing, South Australia’s chief vet Skye Freuan said it was likely the first mass mortality event from the disease. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email South Australia also reported three suspected positive cases in other greater crested terns, including one inland at Monarto, suggesting the disease has begun moving away from the coast. The Monarto area is home to several poultry farms. Three silver gulls were also suspected positive, SA authorities said, adding to the first silver gull found a few days ago and confirmed positive by the CSIRO earlier on Saturday. Kate Millar, the chief executive of conservation charity BirdLife Australia, called it a “very significant escalation of the bird flu situation in Australia, and a very bleak milestone”. “Sadly, we’re at the beginning of a long and challenging battle and birds and wildlife are going to need all the help they can get,” she said. Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said it now appeared the disease was “starting to take off” and “mirroring the experience in South America of early detections, then rapid increases in numbers and spread leading to mass mortality events in wildlife.” “We are still at the very early stages of this devastating disease spreading, but the possible first mass mortality coming just days after the virus was declared not eradicable indicates how quickly this could escalate,” he said. Freuan said there was “nothing we can do” to stop the spread of the disease, but that surveillance was working. The news came at the end of a significant week in the development of the disease when numbers jumped by 20 in just a few days to the current total of 53. Australia was the last continent to have the unwelcome arrival of a disease that has killed millions of birds and mammals around the world. Victoria this week confirmed its first cases of the virulent strain in a greater crested tern found in Portland, with the state joining Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland that have all recorded positive cases. On Saturday, Victorian authorities said samples from five crested terns had been sent to the CSIRO laboratory in Geelong, with preliminary testing suggesting more positive results. Five confirmed cases in birds at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island also raised concerns for the welfare of the area’s Australian sea lions – an endangered species. Tens of thousands of seals have died worldwide from the disease. But it has been the cases among silver gulls that has experts like Sean Dooley, the national affairs adviser at BirdLife Australia, concerned that the spread of the virus has now reached a critical new stage. “When people think of a seagull, they’re almost always thinking of the silver gull,” said Dooley. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Australian sea lions, an endangered species, are at risk of contracting H5N1 bird flu. Photograph: Brad Leue/Alamy “They’re very common, and primarily they are coastal, but they do come inland and can turn up in Lake Eyre following floods,” said Dooley. Silver gulls are the second Australian native species to catch the disease, after dozens of detections in greater crested terns. But it is the silver gull’s behaviour and habits that have experts concerned because they scavenge from dead or dying animals, meaning they can easily pick up the disease from other sick birds. They also pick detritus from water bodies – lakes and flooded areas included – and these are known to be breeding grounds for the disease. “There is such a large population of silver gulls, and they move into other habitats. They could be the vector that takes bird flu inland,” says Dooley. “They’re also really successful in urban areas and could bring the disease into those bird populations.” Because Australia has a high concentration of unique birds, the susceptibility of many native species isn’t known. But the fears are there is no reason to think they would manage any better than birds overseas. Birds that flock around water have tended to be the hardest hit. Examples include sandwich terns, black-headed gulls and northern gannets in Europe and, in Peru, pelicans. Dooley said the mood at BirdLife Australia this week had been one of “trying to suppress that sinking, gut-churning feeling”. The winter season for birdwatchers along the coast had been one of the best in 10 years, said Dooley, with rare petrels turning up in numbers along the east coast. “Now that has been heavily tinged because probably among those were birds carrying H5N1.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu Wildlife Birds Marine life Animals news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light
